chunks.title: Broker FAQ: Submissions and Conditions
chunks.section: When are conditions due and who signs them off?
chunks.text:
## When are conditions due and who signs them off?

Every condition must be met, and the supporting document must be in the loan system, at least 10 business days before the closing date (see PRC-003). The approval states the due date. The Underwriter signs off the appraisal, the down payment and gift letter, the income documents and the insurance confirmation. Mortgage Operations signs off the home insurance proof, the payout statements and discharges, and the lawyer's title confirmation. If a document arrives after the due date, it may still be accepted, but Mortgage Operations must be told at once because the closing may have to be moved. Conditions cannot be waived, and you should not tell the borrower that a late condition will not affect the closing.

chunks.title: Down Payment Requirements and Sources
chunks.section: Example: minimum down payment on a 600,000 purchase
chunks.text:
## Example: minimum down payment on a 600,000 purchase

A borrower is buying a home for 600,000. The first 400,000 of the price needs 6%, which is 24,000. The remaining 200,000 needs 12%, which is 24,000. The minimum down payment is 24,000 + 24,000 = 48,000, which is 8% of the price. The borrower's loan amount cannot be more than 552,000. Now take a purchase of 1,200,000. The price is at the high-price threshold, so the minimum is 20% of the whole price, which is 240,000, and the tiered calculation is not used. For a purchase of 1,000,000, the minimum is 6% of 400,000 plus 12% of 600,000, which is 24,000 + 72,000 = 96,000. In each case the Underwriter compares the minimum with the money the borrower can show from accepted sources and records both amounts in the file.

chunks.title: Underwriting Workflow
chunks.section: Stage 6: Policy tests on ratios, LTV and down payment
chunks.text:
## Stage 6: Policy tests on ratios, LTV and down payment

The Underwriter calculates the qualifying rate under POL-004, then the GDS and TDS ratios under POL-003, the loan-to-value ratio under POL-007 and the minimum down payment under POL-005. The ratios must be at or below 35% for GDS and 42% for TDS. The loan-to-value must be at or below the conventional limit of 80% or be covered by mortgage default insurance, and it must also be within any lower product limit. The maximum amortization is 25 years for an insured mortgage and 30 years for an uninsured mortgage. The Underwriter records every result and the figures used. A file that passes every test goes to the authority check. A file that fails a test that can be excepted goes to the authority check with the failed test noted. A file that fails a test that cannot be excepted is declined.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.text: This policy sets the maximum gross debt service (GDS) ratio at 35% and the maximum total debt service (TDS) ratio at 42%. It defines what counts in each ratio and requires both ratios to use the qualifying rate from POL-004.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: Why both ratios use the qualifying rate
chunks.text:
## Why both ratios use the qualifying rate

GDS and TDS must be calculated with the qualifying rate defined in POL-004, not with the contract rate the borrower will actually pay. The qualifying rate is the greater of the contract rate plus 1.75 points or 5.40%. Using it tests whether the borrower could still afford the mortgage if payments rose. The mortgage payment in both ratios is calculated on the full loan amount, using the amortization allowed for the file and the payment method in POL-012. Underwriting may not use a lower rate, a longer amortization or a smaller loan amount to bring a ratio under the limit. If the calculation changes because the loan amount or the contract rate changes before closing, the Underwriter must recalculate both ratios.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.text:
## GDS and TDS limits

The gross debt service ratio (GDS) may not exceed 35%. The total debt service ratio (TDS) may not exceed 42%. Both limits apply to every application, and both must be met. GDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs. TDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs plus all other monthly debt payments. A file that is within the GDS limit but over the TDS limit does not meet POL-003, and neither does a file that is within TDS but over GDS. The Underwriter calculates both ratios on every file, using the income verified under POL-002 and the qualifying rate set in POL-004. The ratio limits in POL-003 version 2.0 replace the earlier limits in POL-003-V1, which apply only to files decided before 2026-09-01.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file
chunks.text:
## Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file

A borrower has gross monthly income of 9,000. The mortgage payment at the qualifying rate is 2,400, the property tax is 350 per month, heating is counted at 100, and the condo fee is 400 per month, of which 50% is counted, or 200. Housing costs are 2,400 + 350 + 100 + 200 = 3,050. GDS is 3,050 / 9,000 = 33.9%, which is within the 35% limit. The borrower also pays 500 per month on a personal loan and a credit card. TDS is (3,050 + 500) / 9,000 = 39.4%, which is within the 42% limit. This hypothetical file meets both limits. If the condo fee were 800, housing costs would be 3,250, GDS would be 36.1%, and the file would be over the GDS limit.

chunks.title: Underwriting Workflow
chunks.section: Stage 6: Policy tests on ratios, LTV and down payment
chunks.text:
## Stage 6: Policy tests on ratios, LTV and down payment

The Underwriter calculates the qualifying rate under POL-004, then the GDS and TDS ratios under POL-003, the loan-to-value ratio under POL-007 and the minimum down payment under POL-005. The ratios must be at or below 35% for GDS and 42% for TDS. The loan-to-value must be at or below the conventional limit of 80% or be covered by mortgage default insurance, and it must also be within any lower product limit. The maximum amortization is 25 years for an insured mortgage and 30 years for an uninsured mortgage. The Underwriter records every result and the figures used. A file that passes every test goes to the authority check. A file that fails a test that can be excepted goes to the authority check with the failed test noted. A file that fails a test that cannot be excepted is declined.

chunks.title: Qualifying Rate
chunks.section: How the qualifying rate is calculated
chunks.text:
## How the qualifying rate is calculated

The qualifying rate is the greater of two figures: the contract rate plus 1.75 points, or 5.40%. The contract rate is the rate the borrower will actually pay on the mortgage. The 1.75 points are a buffer that tests whether the borrower could still afford the payments if rates rose. The 5.40% figure is a floor, so the qualifying rate is never lower than 5.40%, even when the contract rate is low. Underwriting must calculate both figures on every file and use whichever is greater. The qualifying rate is used to calculate the mortgage payment in the GDS and TDS ratios (see POL-003). It is a testing rate only. The borrower never pays it, it never appears in the mortgage terms, and staff may not quote it to a borrower or broker as the rate of the mortgage. Underwriting may not use a lower qualifying rate without an approved exception under POL-010.

chunks.title: Qualifying Rate
chunks.section: Example: qualifying rate for three products
chunks.text:
## Example: qualifying rate for three products

Using the rate sheet effective 2026-11-01, DMC Prime is 4.70%. For FX5-C the contract rate is 4.69%. Contract rate plus 1.75 points is 6.44%, which is greater than 5.40%, so the qualifying rate is 6.44%. For VR5-C the contract rate is prime minus 0.55, which is 4.15%. Contract rate plus 1.75 points is 5.90%, which is greater than 5.40%, so the qualifying rate is 5.90%. For HEL-1 the contract rate is prime plus 0.75, which is 5.45%. Contract rate plus 1.75 points is 7.20%, so the qualifying rate is 7.20%. Now take a hypothetical contract rate of 3.50%. Contract rate plus 1.75 points is 5.25%, which is less than 5.40%, so the floor applies and the qualifying rate is 5.40%.

chunks.title: Renewals and Maturity
chunks.text:
## Renewal notice 120 days before maturity

Mortgage Operations must send a renewal notice to the borrower 120 days before the maturity date of every closed mortgage. The notice states the maturity date, the outstanding balance on that date, the renewal options available, the way to give an instruction and the date by which the instruction must be received. chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.text:
## Rounding rules

Every payment must be rounded to the nearest cent, with a half cent rounded up. Mortgage Operations rounds the regular payment once, after the formula has been applied, and does not round the interest rate or any figure in the middle of the calculation. The accelerated payments are calculated from the rounded monthly payment, and each accelerated payment is then rounded to the cent. Interest charged on each payment date is rounded to the cent. The final payment of the term or of the amortization is adjusted so that the loan balance is exactly zero, so it may differ from the regular payment by a few cents. Rounding differences are never shown to the borrower as fees and are never charged as an extra amount.

chunks.title: Borrower FAQ: Making Your Payments
chunks.section: How often can I make my mortgage payments?
chunks.text:
## How often can I make my mortgage payments?

You can choose monthly payments, semi-monthly payments, bi-weekly payments, weekly payments, accelerated bi-weekly payments or accelerated weekly payments. Monthly means 12 payments a year, semi-monthly means 24, bi-weekly means 26 and weekly means 52. The two accelerated choices also mean 26 and 52 payments a year. An accelerated bi-weekly payment is half of your monthly payment, and an accelerated weekly payment is one quarter of your monthly payment (see POL-012). Because there are more payment dates in a year, accelerated payments pay your mortgage off faster than the matching standard choice. If you have a home equity line of credit, HEL-1, your minimum payment is the interest charged each month and is set out in PRD-005. Each payment is rounded to the cent.

chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.text:
## The amortization payment formula

Mortgage Operations must calculate the regular payment of a Demo Mortgage Co. mortgage with the amortization formula: payment = P x i / (1 - (1 + i)^(-n)). In the formula P is the loan amount, i is the interest rate for one payment period written as a decimal, and n is the total number of payments over the amortization period. The result is the level payment that repays the loan in full by the end of the amortization period. The amortization period is limited by POL-007. The same formula is used for the payment shown to the borrower and for the payment used in the debt service ratios of POL-003, except that the ratios use the qualifying rate from POL-004 in effect of the contract rate. Staff may not use a different formula, a rounded interest rate or a spreadsheet shortcut that gives a different result.

chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.section: Example: monthly payment on an FX5-C mortgage
chunks.text:
## Example: monthly payment on an FX5-C mortgage

A borrower has an FX5-C mortgage of 400,000 at a contract rate of 4.69%, amortized over 25 years with monthly payments. The fixed rate is compounded semi-annually, so the monthly rate is i = (1 + 0.0469 / 2)^(2 / 12) - 1 = 0.003871. The number of payments is n = 300. The payment is 400,000 x 0.003871 / (1 - (1.003871)^(-300)) = 2,256.34, rounded to the cent. The accelerated bi-weekly payment is 2,256.34 / 2 = 1,128.17 and the accelerated weekly payment is 2,256.34 / 4 = 564.09. For a VR5-C mortgage of 400,000 at 4.15%, the monthly rate is 0.0415 / 12 = 0.003458, and the payment over 25 years is 2,144.62.

chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.text:
## Compounding: fixed semi-annual, variable monthly

The rate for one payment period depends on how the interest rate is compounded. For a fixed-rate mortgage, the stated annual rate is compounded semi-annually. Mortgage Operations converts it to a payment-period rate with the formula i = (1 + r / 2)^(2 / f) - 1, where r is the stated annual rate as a decimal and f is the number of payments per year. For a variable-rate mortgage, the stated annual rate is compounded monthly, and the payment-period rate for monthly payments is i = r / 12. For variable-rate payments made more often than monthly, the monthly rate is converted to the payment period in the same way. The compounding rule applies to FX5-C, FX3-C, SEA-5, RNT-4 and FX1-O as fixed-rate products, and to VR5-C as a variable-rate product. The home equity line of credit HEL-1 calculates interest as stated in PRD-005.

chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.text:
## Rounding rules

Every payment must be rounded to the nearest cent, with a half cent rounded up. Mortgage Operations rounds the regular payment once, after the formula has been applied, and does not round the interest rate or any figure in the middle of the calculation. The accelerated payments are calculated from the rounded monthly payment, and each accelerated payment is then rounded to the cent. Interest charged on each payment date is rounded to the cent. The final payment of the term or of the amortization is adjusted so that the loan balance is exactly zero, so it may differ from the regular payment by a few cents. Rounding differences are never shown to the borrower as fees and are never charged as an extra amount.

chunks.title: Borrower FAQ: Making Your Payments
chunks.section: How often can I make my mortgage payments?
chunks.text:
## How often can I make my mortgage payments?

You can choose monthly payments, semi-monthly payments, bi-weekly payments, weekly payments, accelerated bi-weekly payments or accelerated weekly payments. Monthly means 12 payments a year, semi-monthly means 24, bi-weekly means 26 and weekly means 52. The two accelerated choices also mean 26 and 52 payments a year. An accelerated bi-weekly payment is half of your monthly payment, and an accelerated weekly payment is one quarter of your monthly payment (see POL-012). Because there are more payment dates in a year, accelerated payments pay your mortgage off faster than the matching standard choice. If you have a home equity line of credit, HEL-1, your minimum payment is the interest charged each month and is set out in PRD-005. Each payment is rounded to the cent.

chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.text:
## The amortization payment formula

Mortgage Operations must calculate the regular payment of a Demo Mortgage Co. mortgage with the amortization formula: payment = P x i / (1 - (1 + i)^(-n)). In the formula P is the loan amount, i is the interest rate for one payment period written as a decimal, and n is the total number of payments over the amortization period. The result is the level payment that repays the loan in full by the end of the amortization period. The amortization period is limited by POL-007. The same formula is used for the payment shown to the borrower and for the payment used in the debt service ratios of POL-003, except that the ratios use the qualifying rate from POL-004 in effect of the contract rate. Staff may not use a different formula, a rounded interest rate or a spreadsheet shortcut that gives a different result.

chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.section: Example: monthly payment on an FX5-C mortgage
chunks.text:
## Example: monthly payment on an FX5-C mortgage

A borrower has an FX5-C mortgage of 400,000 at a contract rate of 4.69%, amortized over 25 years with monthly payments. The fixed rate is compounded semi-annually, so the monthly rate is i = (1 + 0.0469 / 2)^(2 / 12) - 1 = 0.003871. The number of payments is n = 300. The payment is 400,000 x 0.003871 / (1 - (1.003871)^(-300)) = 2,256.34, rounded to the cent. The accelerated bi-weekly payment is 2,256.34 / 2 = 1,128.17 and the accelerated weekly payment is 2,256.34 / 4 = 564.09. For a VR5-C mortgage of 400,000 at 4.15%, the monthly rate is 0.0415 / 12 = 0.003458, and the payment over 25 years is 2,144.62.

chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.text:
## Compounding: fixed semi-annual, variable monthly

The rate for one payment period depends on how the interest rate is compounded. For a fixed-rate mortgage, the stated annual rate is compounded semi-annually. Mortgage Operations converts it to a payment-period rate with the formula i = (1 + r / 2)^(2 / f) - 1, where r is the stated annual rate as a decimal and f is the number of payments per year. For a variable-rate mortgage, the stated annual rate is compounded monthly, and the payment-period rate for monthly payments is i = r / 12. For variable-rate payments made more often than monthly, the monthly rate is converted to the payment period in the same way. The compounding rule applies to FX5-C, FX3-C, SEA-5, RNT-4 and FX1-O as fixed-rate products, and to VR5-C as a variable-rate product. The home equity line of credit HEL-1 calculates interest as stated in PRD-005.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.text: This policy sets the maximum gross debt service (GDS) ratio at 35% and the maximum total debt service (TDS) ratio at 42%. It defines what counts in each ratio and requires both ratios to use the qualifying rate from POL-004.

chunks.title: Underwriting Workflow
chunks.section: Stage 6: Policy tests on ratios, LTV and down payment
chunks.text:
## Stage 6: Policy tests on ratios, LTV and down payment

The Underwriter calculates the qualifying rate under POL-004, then the GDS and TDS ratios under POL-003, the loan-to-value ratio under POL-007 and the minimum down payment under POL-005. The ratios must be at or below 35% for GDS and 42% for TDS. The loan-to-value must be at or below the conventional limit of 80% or be covered by mortgage default insurance, and it must also be within any lower product limit. The maximum amortization is 25 years for an insured mortgage and 30 years for an uninsured mortgage. The Underwriter records every result and the figures used. A file that passes every test goes to the authority check. A file that fails a test that can be excepted goes to the authority check with the failed test noted. A file that fails a test that cannot be excepted is declined.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: Why both ratios use the qualifying rate
chunks.text:
## Why both ratios use the qualifying rate

GDS and TDS must be calculated with the qualifying rate defined in POL-004, not with the contract rate the borrower will actually pay. The qualifying rate is the greater of the contract rate plus 1.75 points or 5.40%. Using it tests whether the borrower could still afford the mortgage if payments rose. The mortgage payment in both ratios is calculated on the full loan amount, using the amortization allowed for the file and the payment method in POL-012. Underwriting may not use a lower rate, a longer amortization or a smaller loan amount to bring a ratio under the limit. If the calculation changes because the loan amount or the contract rate changes before closing, the Underwriter must recalculate both ratios.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.text:
## GDS and TDS limits

The gross debt service ratio (GDS) may not exceed 35%. The total debt service ratio (TDS) may not exceed 42%. Both limits apply to every application, and both must be met. GDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs. TDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs plus all other monthly debt payments. A file that is within the GDS limit but over the TDS limit does not meet POL-003, and neither does a file that is within TDS but over GDS. The Underwriter calculates both ratios on every file, using the income verified under POL-002 and the qualifying rate set in POL-004. The ratio limits in POL-003 version 2.0 replace the earlier limits in POL-003-V1, which apply only to files decided before 2026-09-01.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file
chunks.text:
## Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file

A borrower has gross monthly income of 9,000. The mortgage payment at the qualifying rate is 2,400, the property tax is 350 per month, heating is counted at 100, and the condo fee is 400 per month, of which 50% is counted, or 200. Housing costs are 2,400 + 350 + 100 + 200 = 3,050. GDS is 3,050 / 9,000 = 33.9%, which is within the 35% limit. The borrower also pays 500 per month on a personal loan and a credit card. TDS is (3,050 + 500) / 9,000 = 39.4%, which is within the 42% limit. This hypothetical file meets both limits. If the condo fee were 800, housing costs would be 3,250, GDS would be 36.1%, and the file would be over the GDS limit.

chunks.title: Approval Authority Matrix
chunks.text:
## Exception approval authority

The authority to approve exceptions is the same as in POL-010 and is applied through PRC-005. A Senior Underwriter may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted. A Senior Underwriter may approve an income-document exception and a rate hold extension. The Credit Committee approves a loan-to-value exception, and may waive the rate hold extension fee. An Underwriter approves no exception. Privacy rules, fraud flags, property eligibility, the borrowed down payment ban, the qualifying rate, the minimum down payment and the maximum amortization can never be excepted by any role.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.section: Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception
chunks.text:
## Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception

Approval authority for a GDS or TDS exception depends on how far the ratio is over the limit in POL-003. The overage is the ratio minus its limit, measured in points, and where both ratios are over their limits the larger overage decides. A Senior Underwriter may approve an exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve an exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. An Underwriter may not approve any exception, but may prepare the request and recommend it. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted, and the file must be declined or restructured. The role that approves must be named on the EXC-100 and must record the decision, the date and the reasons. The authority limits for loan amounts are separate and are set out in PRC-004.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.section: Who can approve LTV, income document and rate hold exceptions
chunks.text:
## Who can approve LTV, income document and rate hold exceptions

A Senior Underwriter may approve an exception to the income documents required by POL-002 or POL-008, and an exception that extends a rate hold under RATE-003. An exception to the loan-to-value limit in POL-007 or to a product limit must be approved by the Credit Committee. A rate hold extension also needs the extension fee set out in RATE-002 unless the Credit Committee waives it. An approval is for the specific exception named on the EXC-100 and is valid only for the file and the facts described in the request. If the facts change, for example if the loan amount or the property changes, the approval lapses and the Underwriter must raise a new request.

chunks.title: Approval Authority Matrix
chunks.text:
## Example: routing three files

A file for a loan of 600,000 meets every policy. An Underwriter may approve it. A file for a loan of 1,100,000 meets every policy. It is above the Underwriter limit and within the Senior Underwriter limit, so a Senior Underwriter approves it. A file for a loan of 600,000 has a TDS ratio 3.0 points over the limit. The loan amount is within the Underwriter limit, but the exception is above the Senior Underwriter limit of 2.0 points, so the Credit Committee must approve the exception before the file can be approved. A file for a loan of 1,700,000 that meets every policy goes to the Credit Committee because of the loan amount, even though no exception is needed. In each case the Underwriter records the loan amount, the authority limit that applies and the role that approved the file in the loan system.

chunks.title: Underwriting Workflow
chunks.text:
## Stage 7: Authority check

The Underwriter checks that the loan amount is within the authority of the role that will approve the file. An Underwriter may approve a loan amount up to 750,000, a Senior Underwriter up to 1,500,000, and the Credit Committee any amount above that (see PRC-004). If the amount is above the Underwriter's authority, the file is passed to a Senior Underwriter or to the Credit Committee for approval. If a policy test has failed and the failure can be excepted, the Underwriter prepares an EXC-100 under PRC-005, with the loan number, the exception type, the requested value, the justification and the compensating factors. The Underwriter recommends but does not approve any exception. The file stays in a pending-approval status until a human with the right authority approves the exception. Nobody may approve an exception verbally.

| Income documents | Senior Underwriter |
| Rate hold extension | Senior Underwriter |

chunks.title: Approval Authority Matrix
chunks.text:
## Exception approval authority

The authority to approve exceptions is the same as in POL-010 and is applied through PRC-005. A Senior Underwriter may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted. A Senior Underwriter may approve an income-document exception and a rate hold extension. The Credit Committee approves a loan-to-value exception, and may waive the rate hold extension fee. An Underwriter approves no exception. Privacy rules, fraud flags, property eligibility, the borrowed down payment ban, the qualifying rate, the minimum down payment and the maximum amortization can never be excepted by any role.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.section: Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception
chunks.text:
## Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception

Approval authority for a GDS or TDS exception depends on how far the ratio is over the limit in POL-003. The overage is the ratio minus its limit, measured in points, and where both ratios are over their limits the larger overage decides. A Senior Underwriter may approve an exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve an exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. An Underwriter may not approve any exception, but may prepare the request and recommend it. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted, and the file must be declined or restructured. The role that approves must be named on the EXC-100 and must record the decision, the date and the reasons. The authority limits for loan amounts are separate and are set out in PRC-004.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.section: Example: which role approves which overage
chunks.text:
## Example: which role approves which overage

A file has a GDS of 36.1% and a TDS of 39.4%. The GDS limit is 35%, so the GDS overage is 1.1 points. The TDS is under its limit. The larger overage is 1.1 points, so a Senior Underwriter may approve the exception. A second file has a TDS of 45.0%. The TDS limit is 42%, so the overage is 3.0 points, which is above 2.0 points and not above 4.0 points. The Credit Committee must approve it. A third file has a GDS of 39.5%. The overage is 4.5 points, which is above 4.0 points, so the file cannot be excepted and must be declined or restructured. For the first two files the Underwriter prepares the EXC-100 with the loan number, both ratios, the overage in points and the compensating factors, and sends it to the role that has authority for the overage, as described in PRC-005.

chunks.title: Exception Request Procedure
chunks.text:
## Routing by authority

The Underwriter routes each EXC-100 to the role that has authority, using the table below. The routing is the same as the approval authority in POL-010 and PRC-004.

| Exception | Approver |
| --- | --- |
| GDS or TDS up to 2.0 points over the limit | Senior Underwriter |
| GDS or TDS more than 2.0 and up to 4.0 points over the limit | Credit Committee |
| GDS or TDS more than 4.0 points over the limit | Cannot be excepted |
| Loan-to-value | Credit Committee |
| Income documents | Senior Underwriter |
| Rate hold extension | Senior Underwriter |

Where both GDS and TDS are over their limits, the larger overage decides the route. A rate hold extension also carries the extension fee in RATE-002, which only the Credit Committee may waive. An Underwriter prepares and recommends the request but approves no exception.

chunks.title: Approval Authority Matrix
chunks.text:
## Example: routing three files

A file for a loan of 600,000 meets every policy. An Underwriter may approve it. A file for a loan of 1,100,000 meets every policy. It is above the Underwriter limit and within the Senior Underwriter limit, so a Senior Underwriter approves it. A file for a loan of 600,000 has a TDS ratio 3.0 points over the limit. The loan amount is within the Underwriter limit, but the exception is above the Senior Underwriter limit of 2.0 points, so the Credit Committee must approve the exception before the file can be approved. A file for a loan of 1,700,000 that meets every policy goes to the Credit Committee because of the loan amount, even though no exception is needed. In each case the Underwriter records the loan amount, the authority limit that applies and the role that approved the file in the loan system.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.text: This policy sets the maximum gross debt service (GDS) ratio at 35% and the maximum total debt service (TDS) ratio at 42%. It defines what counts in each ratio and requires both ratios to use the qualifying rate from POL-004.

chunks.title: Underwriting Workflow
chunks.section: Stage 6: Policy tests on ratios, LTV and down payment
chunks.text:
## Stage 6: Policy tests on ratios, LTV and down payment

The Underwriter calculates the qualifying rate under POL-004, then the GDS and TDS ratios under POL-003, the loan-to-value ratio under POL-007 and the minimum down payment under POL-005. The ratios must be at or below 35% for GDS and 42% for TDS. The loan-to-value must be at or below the conventional limit of 80% or be covered by mortgage default insurance, and it must also be within any lower product limit. The maximum amortization is 25 years for an insured mortgage and 30 years for an uninsured mortgage. The Underwriter records every result and the figures used. A file that passes every test goes to the authority check. A file that fails a test that can be excepted goes to the authority check with the failed test noted. A file that fails a test that cannot be excepted is declined.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: Why both ratios use the qualifying rate
chunks.text:
## Why both ratios use the qualifying rate

GDS and TDS must be calculated with the qualifying rate defined in POL-004, not with the contract rate the borrower will actually pay. The qualifying rate is the greater of the contract rate plus 1.75 points or 5.40%. Using it tests whether the borrower could still afford the mortgage if payments rose. The mortgage payment in both ratios is calculated on the full loan amount, using the amortization allowed for the file and the payment method in POL-012. Underwriting may not use a lower rate, a longer amortization or a smaller loan amount to bring a ratio under the limit. If the calculation changes because the loan amount or the contract rate changes before closing, the Underwriter must recalculate both ratios.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.text:
## GDS and TDS limits

The gross debt service ratio (GDS) may not exceed 35%. The total debt service ratio (TDS) may not exceed 42%. Both limits apply to every application, and both must be met. GDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs. TDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs plus all other monthly debt payments. A file that is within the GDS limit but over the TDS limit does not meet POL-003, and neither does a file that is within TDS but over GDS. The Underwriter calculates both ratios on every file, using the income verified under POL-002 and the qualifying rate set in POL-004. The ratio limits in POL-003 version 2.0 replace the earlier limits in POL-003-V1, which apply only to files decided before 2026-09-01.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file
chunks.text:
## Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file

A borrower has gross monthly income of 9,000. The mortgage payment at the qualifying rate is 2,400, the property tax is 350 per month, heating is counted at 100, and the condo fee is 400 per month, of which 50% is counted, or 200. Housing costs are 2,400 + 350 + 100 + 200 = 3,050. GDS is 3,050 / 9,000 = 33.9%, which is within the 35% limit. The borrower also pays 500 per month on a personal loan and a credit card. TDS is (3,050 + 500) / 9,000 = 39.4%, which is within the 42% limit. This hypothetical file meets both limits. If the condo fee were 800, housing costs would be 3,250, GDS would be 36.1%, and the file would be over the GDS limit.

chunks.title: Payment Calculation Method
chunks.text:
## Payment frequencies

The borrower may choose among these payment frequencies: monthly with 12 payments per year, semi-monthly with 24, bi-weekly with 26, weekly with 52, accelerated bi-weekly with 26 and accelerated weekly with 52. For the standard frequencies, Mortgage Operations applies the formula in POL-012 with f set to the number of payments per year. For an accelerated frequency, the payment is based on the monthly payment: accelerated bi-weekly is half of the monthly payment, and accelerated weekly is one quarter of the monthly payment. Because there are more payment periods in a year than in the standard schedule, the accelerated frequencies repay the loan faster than the matching standard frequencies. A change of payment frequency after closing carries the fee shown in RATE-002 and takes effect from the next payment date.

chunks.title: Borrower FAQ: Making Your Payments
chunks.section: How often can I make my mortgage payments?
chunks.text:
## How often can I make my mortgage payments?

You can choose monthly payments, semi-monthly payments, bi-weekly payments, weekly payments, accelerated bi-weekly payments or accelerated weekly payments. Monthly means 12 payments a year, semi-monthly means 24, bi-weekly means 26 and weekly means 52. The two accelerated choices also mean 26 and 52 payments a year. An accelerated bi-weekly payment is half of your monthly payment, and an accelerated weekly payment is one quarter of your monthly payment (see POL-012). Because there are more payment dates in a year, accelerated payments pay your mortgage off faster than the matching standard choice. If you have a home equity line of credit, HEL-1, your minimum payment is the interest charged each month and is set out in PRD-005. Each payment is rounded to the cent.

chunks.title: 5-Year Fixed Closed (FX5-C)
chunks.text:
## FX5-C payment frequencies

A borrower with an FX5-C mortgage may choose monthly, semi-monthly, bi-weekly, weekly, accelerated bi-weekly or accelerated weekly payments. Mortgage Operations calculates every FX5-C payment under POL-012, with fixed-rate interest compounded semi-annually, and rounds each payment to the cent. The accelerated frequencies are based on the monthly payment, so they repay the FX5-C mortgage faster than the matching standard frequencies. The borrower chooses the frequency on the application. A later change of payment frequency or payment date carries the payment change fee in RATE-002 and takes effect from the next payment date. A missed or returned payment may carry the NSF fee in RATE-002. Staff must tell the borrower which frequency is in the mortgage terms, and must not describe an accelerated frequency as a different product or as a way to avoid the prepayment limits in POL-009.

chunks.section: Example: monthly payment on an FX5-C mortgage
chunks.text:
## Example: monthly payment on an FX5-C mortgage

A borrower has an FX5-C mortgage of 400,000 at a contract rate of 4.69%, amortized over 25 years with monthly payments. The fixed rate is compounded semi-annually, so the monthly rate is i = (1 + 0.0469 / 2)^(2 / 12) - 1 = 0.003871. The number of payments is n = 300. The payment is 400,000 x 0.003871 / (1 - (1.003871)^(-300)) = 2,256.34, rounded to the cent. The accelerated bi-weekly payment is 2,256.34 / 2 = 1,128.17 and the accelerated weekly payment is 2,256.34 / 4 = 564.09. For a VR5-C mortgage of 400,000 at 4.15%, the monthly rate is 0.0415 / 12 = 0.003458, and the payment over 25 years is 2,144.62.

chunks.title: Approval Authority Matrix
chunks.text:
## Exception approval authority

The authority to approve exceptions is the same as in POL-010 and is applied through PRC-005. A Senior Underwriter may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted. A Senior Underwriter may approve an income-document exception and a rate hold extension. The Credit Committee approves a loan-to-value exception, and may waive the rate hold extension fee. An Underwriter approves no exception. Privacy rules, fraud flags, property eligibility, the borrowed down payment ban, the qualifying rate, the minimum down payment and the maximum amortization can never be excepted by any role.

chunks.text: This policy sets the maximum gross debt service (GDS) ratio at 35% and the maximum total debt service (TDS) ratio at 42%. It defines what counts in each ratio and requires both ratios to use the qualifying rate from POL-004.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.section: Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception
chunks.text:
## Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception

Approval authority for a GDS or TDS exception depends on how far the ratio is over the limit in POL-003. The overage is the ratio minus its limit, measured in points, and where both ratios are over their limits the larger overage decides. A Senior Underwriter may approve an exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve an exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. An Underwriter may not approve any exception, but may prepare the request and recommend it. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted, and the file must be declined or restructured. The role that approves must be named on the EXC-100 and must record the decision, the date and the reasons. The authority limits for loan amounts are separate and are set out in PRC-004.

chunks.title: Exception Request Procedure
chunks.text:
## Routing by authority

The Underwriter routes each EXC-100 to the role that has authority, using the table below. The routing is the same as the approval authority in POL-010 and PRC-004.

| Exception | Approver |
| --- | --- |
| GDS or TDS up to 2.0 points over the limit | Senior Underwriter |
| GDS or TDS more than 2.0 and up to 4.0 points over the limit | Credit Committee |
| GDS or TDS more than 4.0 points over the limit | Cannot be excepted |
| Loan-to-value | Credit Committee |
| Income documents | Senior Underwriter |
| Rate hold extension | Senior Underwriter |

Where both GDS and TDS are over their limits, the larger overage decides the route. A rate hold extension also carries the extension fee in RATE-002, which only the Credit Committee may waive. An Underwriter prepares and recommends the request but approves no exception.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.text:
## GDS and TDS limits

The gross debt service ratio (GDS) may not exceed 35%. The total debt service ratio (TDS) may not exceed 42%. Both limits apply to every application, and both must be met. GDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs. TDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs plus all other monthly debt payments. A file that is within the GDS limit but over the TDS limit does not meet POL-003, and neither does a file that is within TDS but over GDS. The Underwriter calculates both ratios on every file, using the income verified under POL-002 and the qualifying rate set in POL-004. The ratio limits in POL-003 version 2.0 replace the earlier limits in POL-003-V1, which apply only to files decided before 2026-09-01.

chunks.section: Conditions due 10 business days before closing
chunks.text:
## Conditions due 10 business days before closing

Every condition must be met and the supporting document must be in the loan system at least 10 business days before the closing date. The Underwriter states the due date on the approval, calculated from the closing date in the purchase agreement. Mortgage Operations tracks the due date and sends a reminder to the broker or branch. The due date applies to the document being received, not to the borrower promising to provide it. If a document arrives after the due date, the file owner may still accept it but must tell Mortgage Operations at once, because the closing may have to be moved. Conditions that depend on events after the due date, such as the lawyer's final report on title, are listed separately as closing conditions and are checked under PRC-006. Staff may not tell a borrower that a late condition will not affect the closing.

chunks.section: When are conditions due and who signs them off?
chunks.text:
## When are conditions due and who signs them off?

Every condition must be met, and the supporting document must be in the loan system, at least 10 business days before the closing date (see PRC-003). The approval states the due date. The Underwriter signs off the appraisal, the down payment and gift letter, the income documents and the insurance confirmation. Mortgage Operations signs off the home insurance proof, the payout statements and discharges, and the lawyer's title confirmation. If a document arrives after the due date, it may still be accepted, but Mortgage Operations must be told at once because the closing may have to be moved. Conditions cannot be waived, and you should not tell the borrower that a late condition will not affect the closing.

Every condition must be met and the supporting document must be in the loan system at least 10 business days before the closing date. chunks.title: Approval Authority Matrix
chunks.text:
## Exception approval authority

The authority to approve exceptions is the same as in POL-010 and is applied through PRC-005. A Senior Underwriter may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted. A Senior Underwriter may approve an income-document exception and a rate hold extension. The Credit Committee approves a loan-to-value exception, and may waive the rate hold extension fee. An Underwriter approves no exception. Privacy rules, fraud flags, property eligibility, the borrowed down payment ban, the qualifying rate, the minimum down payment and the maximum amortization can never be excepted by any role.

chunks.title: Exception Request Procedure
chunks.text:
## Routing by authority

The Underwriter routes each EXC-100 to the role that has authority, using the table below. The routing is the same as the approval authority in POL-010 and PRC-004.

| Exception | Approver |
| --- | --- |
| GDS or TDS up to 2.0 points over the limit | Senior Underwriter |
| GDS or TDS more than 2.0 and up to 4.0 points over the limit | Credit Committee |
| GDS or TDS more than 4.0 points over the limit | Cannot be excepted |
| Loan-to-value | Credit Committee |
| Income documents | Senior Underwriter |
| Rate hold extension | Senior Underwriter |

Where both GDS and TDS are over their limits, the larger overage decides the route. A rate hold extension also carries the extension fee in RATE-002, which only the Credit Committee may waive. An Underwriter prepares and recommends the request but approves no exception.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.section: Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception
chunks.text:
## Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception

Approval authority for a GDS or TDS exception depends on how far the ratio is over the limit in POL-003. The overage is the ratio minus its limit, measured in points, and where both ratios are over their limits the larger overage decides. A Senior Underwriter may approve an exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve an exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. An Underwriter may not approve any exception, but may prepare the request and recommend it. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted, and the file must be declined or restructured. The role that approves must be named on the EXC-100 and must record the decision, the date and the reasons. The authority limits for loan amounts are separate and are set out in PRC-004.

chunks.section: What happens when a ratio is over the limit
chunks.text:
## What happens when a ratio is over the limit

An Underwriter may not approve a file whose GDS or TDS ratio is over the limit in POL-003. The Underwriter may approve it only after an exception has been requested and approved under POL-010. The exception request is raised on form EXC-100 and is routed to the role that has authority for the size of the overage (see PRC-005). The request must show both ratios, the compensating factors and the justification. A ratio is not rounded down to bring it under the limit; any ratio above the limit, even by a small amount, is over the limit. Staff may not tell a borrower or broker that a file with a ratio over the limit will be approved. They may say that the file needs an exception review and that the review is not a promise of approval.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.text:
## GDS and TDS limits

The gross debt service ratio (GDS) may not exceed 35%. The total debt service ratio (TDS) may not exceed 42%. Both limits apply to every application, and both must be met. GDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs. TDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs plus all other monthly debt payments. A file that is within the GDS limit but over the TDS limit does not meet POL-003, and neither does a file that is within TDS but over GDS. The Underwriter calculates both ratios on every file, using the income verified under POL-002 and the qualifying rate set in POL-004. The ratio limits in POL-003 version 2.0 replace the earlier limits in POL-003-V1, which apply only to files decided before 2026-09-01.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file
chunks.text:
## Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file

A borrower has gross monthly income of 9,000. The mortgage payment at the qualifying rate is 2,400, the property tax is 350 per month, heating is counted at 100, and the condo fee is 400 per month, of which 50% is counted, or 200. Housing costs are 2,400 + 350 + 100 + 200 = 3,050. GDS is 3,050 / 9,000 = 33.9%, which is within the 35% limit. The borrower also pays 500 per month on a personal loan and a credit card. TDS is (3,050 + 500) / 9,000 = 39.4%, which is within the 42% limit. This hypothetical file meets both limits. If the condo fee were 800, housing costs would be 3,250, GDS would be 36.1%, and the file would be over the GDS limit.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: Why both ratios use the qualifying rate
chunks.text:
## Why both ratios use the qualifying rate

GDS and TDS must be calculated with the qualifying rate defined in POL-004, not with the contract rate the borrower will actually pay. The qualifying rate is the greater of the contract rate plus 1.75 points or 5.40%. Using it tests whether the borrower could still afford the mortgage if payments rose. The mortgage payment in both ratios is calculated on the full loan amount, using the amortization allowed for the file and the payment method in POL-012. Underwriting may not use a lower rate, a longer amortization or a smaller loan amount to bring a ratio under the limit. If the calculation changes because the loan amount or the contract rate changes before closing, the Underwriter must recalculate both ratios.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: What counts in the TDS ratio
chunks.text:
## What counts in the TDS ratio

The TDS ratio counts everything in the GDS ratio plus the other monthly debt payments of every borrower on the file. Underwriting must include the minimum monthly payment on each credit card and line of credit, the monthly payment on each loan, any support payments the borrower is required to make, and the payment on any other mortgage. Each payment comes from the credit bureau report or from a statement the borrower supplies. A debt that will be paid off from the proceeds of this mortgage, and that is shown as paid in the instructions to the lawyer, is left out. A debt that the borrower says is paid but that still appears on the credit bureau report must be counted until proof of payment is in the file. The total is divided by gross monthly income to give the TDS ratio.

chunks.title: Income Verification
chunks.section: How old an employment letter may be
chunks.text:
## How old an employment letter may be

An employment letter used to verify income must be dated within 30 days of the credit decision. The date on the letter is the date the employer signed it, not the date the broker or branch received it. If the letter is older than 30 days when the Underwriter reviews the file, the Underwriter must ask for a new letter and may not decide the file on the old one. A letter that is undated or unsigned is treated as missing. The Underwriter may accept a letter sent directly by the employer, or a letter supplied by the borrower that the Underwriter has confirmed with the employer. The Underwriter records how the letter was confirmed. The 30-day limit applies to the employment letter only; the pay stub must simply be recent enough to show the current pay period. Underwriting may not extend the 30-day limit without an approved exception under POL-010.

chunks.title: Underwriting Workflow
chunks.text:
## Stage 3: Income verification

The Underwriter verifies the income of each borrower using the documents required by POL-002 for salaried, variable and rental income, and POL-008 for self-employed income. For a salaried borrower, the Underwriter checks the pay stub and an employment letter dated within 30 days of the decision. For variable income the Underwriter calculates the 2-year average. For rental income the Underwriter counts 50% of gross rents. The Underwriter records each document, the amount counted and the method in the file. Income that cannot be verified is not counted, and the Underwriter tells the broker or branch which document is still needed. If the borrower cannot supply a required income document, the only route is an income-document exception under POL-010, which is decided by the role named in PRC-005.

chunks.title: Broker FAQ: Submissions and Conditions
chunks.section: Which conditions will I see on an approval?
chunks.text:
## Which conditions will I see on an approval?

When Underwriting approves a file with conditions, the conditions are the facts that must still be confirmed before the loan is funded (see PRC-003). The standard conditions are a satisfactory full appraisal, proof that the down payment comes from accepted sources and, for a gift, the signed gift letter, an employment letter dated within 30 days where income depends on it, confirmation from the mortgage default insurer where insurance is needed, proof of home insurance, payout statements and discharge of any debt or mortgage paid from the proceeds, and the lawyer's confirmation of clear title. Underwriting may add a condition specific to the file, and each condition names the document needed and who must supply it.

chunks.title: Income Verification
chunks.text: This policy sets the documents Underwriting must collect to verify income. Salaried borrowers need a recent pay stub and an employment letter dated within 30 days. Variable income is a 2-year average, and 50% of gross rental income is counted.

chunks.title: Income Verification
chunks.text:
## Documents required for salaried income

Underwriting must verify the income of a salaried borrower with two documents: a recent pay stub and an employment letter. The pay stub must show the pay period, the year-to-date earnings and the employer's name. The employment letter must come from the employer, state the borrower's position, employment status, start date and base pay, and be dated within 30 days of the credit decision. The pay stub and the employment letter must agree on base pay. If they differ, the Underwriter must resolve the difference with the borrower before deciding and must note the explanation in the file. Income that is only stated by the borrower, with no document behind it, may not be counted. A salaried borrower with a second salaried job must supply the same two documents for each job, and Underwriting counts each job separately. The ratios that use the verified income are set in POL-003.

chunks.title: Exception Request Procedure
chunks.text:
## EXC-100 fields

The EXC-100 has five required fields, and a request is complete only when all five are filled in. The loan number gives the file in the format DMC-YYYY-NNNNN. The exception type names which of the four items is being excepted. The requested value states the figure being asked for, for example the ratio the file will have, the loan-to-value, the document that will be accepted in place of the required one or the new rate hold end date. The justification explains in plain words why the exception is sensible for this file. The compensating factors list the documented strengths of the file that reduce the risk, as defined in POL-010, and they must not already have been counted in the figure being excepted. The Underwriter attaches the supporting documents. An incomplete EXC-100 is sent back and the decision time does not start.

chunks.title: Exception Request Procedure
chunks.section: When an EXC-100 may be raised
chunks.text:
## When an EXC-100 may be raised

An Underwriter raises an exception request on form EXC-100 when a file fails a test that POL-010 allows to be excepted. Only four things can be excepted: the GDS or TDS ratio limit, the loan-to-value limit, the income documents required by POL-002 or POL-008, and the rate hold period. Nothing else can be excepted. A request must not be raised for privacy rules, fraud flags, property eligibility, a borrowed down payment, the qualifying rate, the minimum down payment or the maximum amortization, and such a file must be declined or stopped. The Underwriter raises the request before the file is approved, not after. A Loan Officer or a broker may ask for an exception, but only an Underwriter may raise the EXC-100. The Underwriter must not tell the borrower that an exception will be granted.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.text:
## Recording and timing of exceptions

The Underwriter must keep the EXC-100, the approval and the supporting documents in the file. An exception is not valid if it is given verbally, by message or by email without an EXC-100 approval in the file. Decisions on exception requests are due within 2 business days of a complete request. The request is complete when it names the loan number, the exception type, the requested value, the justification and the compensating factors (see PRC-005). Credit Risk reviews the exceptions approved in each period and reports to the Credit Committee. Staff may tell a borrower that an exception review is under way, but may not say that it will be approved. The Underwriter must also tell the broker or branch that a pending request is not a commitment to lend, and that the file may not go to closing until the approval is recorded in the file by the role named on the EXC-100.

chunks.title: Exception Request Procedure
chunks.text:
## The 2-business-day decision time

The approver must decide a complete EXC-100 within 2 business days of receiving it. The count starts on the first business day after the EXC-100 is complete in the loan system. The approver records the decision as approved or refused, with the date, the reasons and the compensating factors relied on. If the approver needs more information, the approver returns the request to the Underwriter with the question, and the 2 business days start again when the answer is in the file. Credit Risk reports each period on the number of requests decided inside and outside the time. A request decided late is still valid, but the delay is recorded. Underwriting tells the broker or branch only that a review is under way, and never forecasts the result.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.text:
## Compensating factors

An exception request must show compensating factors, which are documented strengths of the file that reduce the risk created by the exception. Examples are a long and stable employment history, a strong credit bureau record, a larger down payment than the minimum, substantial savings left after closing, low other debts and a long-standing relationship with Demo Mortgage Co. A compensating factor must be documented in the file and must not already have been counted in the ratio or the limit being excepted. A request with no compensating factors, or with factors that are vague or undocumented, must be sent back. The approver must record which factors were relied on. The Credit Committee may require more compensating factors for a larger exception than a Senior Underwriter would.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.section: Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception
chunks.text:
## Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception

Approval authority for a GDS or TDS exception depends on how far the ratio is over the limit in POL-003. The overage is the ratio minus its limit, measured in points, and where both ratios are over their limits the larger overage decides. A Senior Underwriter may approve an exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve an exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. An Underwriter may not approve any exception, but may prepare the request and recommend it. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted, and the file must be declined or restructured. The role that approves must be named on the EXC-100 and must record the decision, the date and the reasons. The authority limits for loan amounts are separate and are set out in PRC-004.

chunks.title: Approval Authority Matrix
chunks.text:
## Exception approval authority

The authority to approve exceptions is the same as in POL-010 and is applied through PRC-005. A Senior Underwriter may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve a GDS or TDS exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted. A Senior Underwriter may approve an income-document exception and a rate hold extension. The Credit Committee approves a loan-to-value exception, and may waive the rate hold extension fee. An Underwriter approves no exception. Privacy rules, fraud flags, property eligibility, the borrowed down payment ban, the qualifying rate, the minimum down payment and the maximum amortization can never be excepted by any role.

chunks.title: Exception Request Procedure
chunks.section: When an EXC-100 may be raised
chunks.text:
## When an EXC-100 may be raised

An Underwriter raises an exception request on form EXC-100 when a file fails a test that POL-010 allows to be excepted. Only four things can be excepted: the GDS or TDS ratio limit, the loan-to-value limit, the income documents required by POL-002 or POL-008, and the rate hold period. Nothing else can be excepted. A request must not be raised for privacy rules, fraud flags, property eligibility, a borrowed down payment, the qualifying rate, the minimum down payment or the maximum amortization, and such a file must be declined or stopped. The Underwriter raises the request before the file is approved, not after. A Loan Officer or a broker may ask for an exception, but only an Underwriter may raise the EXC-100. The Underwriter must not tell the borrower that an exception will be granted.

chunks.title: Debt Service Ratio Limits (GDS/TDS)
chunks.section: What happens when a ratio is over the limit
chunks.text:
## What happens when a ratio is over the limit

An Underwriter may not approve a file whose GDS or TDS ratio is over the limit in POL-003. The Underwriter may approve it only after an exception has been requested and approved under POL-010. The exception request is raised on form EXC-100 and is routed to the role that has authority for the size of the overage (see PRC-005). The request must show both ratios, the compensating factors and the justification. A ratio is not rounded down to bring it under the limit; any ratio above the limit, even by a small amount, is over the limit. Staff may not tell a borrower or broker that a file with a ratio over the limit will be approved. They may say that the file needs an exception review and that the review is not a promise of approval.

chunks.title: Exceptions to Credit Policy
chunks.text:
## Items that can be excepted

Only four items in the Demo Mortgage Co. credit policy can be excepted. They are the GDS and TDS ratio limits in POL-003, the loan-to-value limits in POL-007, the income documents required by POL-002 and POL-008, and the rate hold period in RATE-003. Any rule that is not on that list cannot be excepted by any role. That includes the qualifying rate in POL-004, the minimum down payment and its sources in POL-005, the property types in POL-006 and the maximum amortization in POL-007. An exception changes the requirement for one file only. It does not change the policy, and it does not set a precedent for another file. Every exception must be requested on form EXC-100 and approved before the file is approved (see PRC-005). A request stays pending until a human with the right authority approves it.

## Who can approve a GDS or TDS exception

Approval authority for a GDS or TDS exception depends on how far the ratio is over the limit in POL-003. The overage is the ratio minus its limit, measured in points, and where both ratios are over their limits the larger overage decides. A Senior Underwriter may approve an exception of up to 2.0 points over the limit. The Credit Committee may approve an exception of up to 4.0 points over the limit. An Underwriter may not approve any exception, but may prepare the request and recommend it. A ratio more than 4.0 points over the limit cannot be excepted, and the file must be declined or restructured. The role that approves must be named on the EXC-100 and must record the decision, the date and the reasons. The authority limits for loan amounts are separate and are set out in PRC-004.

## Compensating factors

An exception request must show compensating factors, which are documented strengths of the file that reduce the risk created by the exception. Examples are a long and stable employment history, a strong credit bureau record, a larger down payment than the minimum, substantial savings left after closing, low other debts and a long-standing relationship with Demo Mortgage Co. A compensating factor must be documented in the file and must not already have been counted in the ratio or the limit being excepted. A request with no compensating factors, or with factors that are vague or undocumented, must be sent back. The approver must record which factors were relied on. The Credit Committee may require more compensating factors for a larger exception than a Senior Underwriter would.

| GDS or TDS more than 4.0 points over the limit | Cannot be excepted |
| Loan-to-value | Credit Committee |
| Income documents | Senior Underwriter |
| Rate hold extension | Senior Underwriter |

## GDS and TDS limits

The gross debt service ratio (GDS) may not exceed 35%. The total debt service ratio (TDS) may not exceed 42%. Both limits apply to every application, and both must be met. GDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs. TDS measures the share of gross monthly income that goes to housing costs plus all other monthly debt payments. A file that is within the GDS limit but over the TDS limit does not meet POL-003, and neither does a file that is within TDS but over GDS. The Underwriter calculates both ratios on every file, using the income verified under POL-002 and the qualifying rate set in POL-004. The ratio limits in POL-003 version 2.0 replace the earlier limits in POL-003-V1, which apply only to files decided before 2026-09-01.

## Example: GDS and TDS for a sample condominium file

A borrower has gross monthly income of 9,000. The mortgage payment at the qualifying rate is 2,400, the property tax is 350 per month, heating is counted at 100, and the condo fee is 400 per month, of which 50% is counted, or 200. Housing costs are 2,400 + 350 + 100 + 200 = 3,050. GDS is 3,050 / 9,000 = 33.9%, which is within the 35% limit. The borrower also pays 500 per month on a personal loan and a credit card. TDS is (3,050 + 500) / 9,000 = 39.4%, which is within the 42% limit. This hypothetical file meets both limits. If the condo fee were 800, housing costs would be 3,250, GDS would be 36.1%, and the file would be over the GDS limit.

An Underwriter raises an exception request on form EXC-100 when a file fails a test that POL-010 allows to be excepted.
